name: Beretta M9 pistol
note: 9 mm semi-automatic pistol built on the Beretta 92 design. The standard U.S. military sidearm of its era.

credit.creator: PEO Soldier (U.S. Army), via the U.S. Air Force Flickr stream

name: M16A1 rifle
note: 5.56 mm rifle of the A1 pattern: triangular handguard, simple A1 rear sight and a forward assist.

credit.creator: Sgt. James Stanfield, U.S. Marine Corps (National Museum of the Marine Corps collection)

name: M4 carbine
caption: Shown with the rail adapter system handguard
note: 5.56 mm carbine: a shorter, lighter member of the M16 family with a collapsible stock. His own M4 in Iraq (March 2006) carried a Knight's RIS quad rail, an EOTech holographic weapon sight (likely a 552), a forward rail grip area, a tan single-point sling and field-applied desert spray paint. The card photo is a PEO Soldier M4 with the rail system, not his rifle.

name: Centurion C-RAM
caption: Trailer-mounted, with its generator (Iraq)
note: Counter-Rocket, Artillery, Mortar (C-RAM) weapon: the Navy's Phalanx close-in weapon system, a radar-guided 20 mm Gatling gun, mounted on a trailer for use ashore. It is built to shoot down incoming rockets, artillery and mortar rounds over a base.

credit.creator: Alpha Battery, 1st Battalion, 194th Field Artillery (U.S. Army National Guard)

name: Up-armored HMMWV with turtleback
caption: M1114 shown, with the armored gunner’s turret
note: Up-armored Humvee with armored doors and glass, and an armored gunner’s turret on the roof, the “turtleback”.

credit.creator: Sgt. Shannon Yount, U.S. Marine Corps

name: CUCV
caption: CUCV pickup shown
note: Commercial Utility Cargo Vehicle: militarized Chevrolet diesel trucks (M1008 pickup, M1009 Blazer and variants) used as light utility vehicles.

credit.creator: TSgt. Rob Marshall, U.S. Air Force

name: Toyota Hilux pickup
caption: White, unarmored (double cab shown)
note: Unarmored white Toyota Hilux pickup, the civilian truck widely used in Iraq and Afghanistan.

credit.creator: Rutger van der Maar (Flickr), via Wikimedia Commons

name: Toyota Land Cruiser, up-armored
caption: Dark blue Land Cruiser 200 shown (armoring is not visible from outside)
note: Armored Toyota Land Cruiser SUV: a civilian-looking vehicle fitted with armor and bullet-resistant glass.

name: Zodiac
caption: Combat rubber raiding craft (F470), ashore
note: Combat rubber raiding craft, the Zodiac F470 inflatable boat. Run with an outboard motor or paddled.

credit.creator: Cpl. Jonathan Rodriguez Pastrana, U.S. Marine Corps

name: USS Frank Cable (AS-40)
note: Emory S. Land-class submarine tender, built to repair and resupply submarines alongside.

credit.creator: Photographer's Mate 3rd Class Ian W. Anderson, U.S. Navy

name: USS Tortuga (LSD-46)
note: Whidbey Island-class dock landing ship: carries Marines, their vehicles and landing craft, and launches the craft from a floodable well deck.

credit.creator: Photographer's Mate 1st Class Martin Maddock, U.S. Navy

name: LCAC (Landing Craft Air Cushion)
caption: Entering USS Tortuga’s well deck, 2007
note: Landing Craft Air Cushion: a hovercraft that carries Marines, vehicles and cargo from a well deck to the beach. Whidbey Island-class LSDs such as Tortuga (LSD-46) embark LCACs in the well deck. Card photo: an LCAC preparing to enter Tortuga off Okinawa, 1 March 2007.

credit.creator: Mass Communication Specialist Seaman Brandon Myrick, U.S. Navy (2007)

name: USS Essex (LHD-2)
note: Wasp-class amphibious assault ship: a flight deck for helicopters and Harrier or F-35B jets, and a well deck for landing craft.

credit.creator: Mass Communication Specialist Seaman Adam K. Thomas, U.S. Navy

name: PASGT helmet, desert cover
caption: 3-color desert (DCU) cover
note: Personnel Armor System for Ground Troops (PASGT) helmet, the Kevlar “K-pot” the U.S. Army and Marine Corps fielded in the early 1980s. It protects the head, temples, ears and neck against fragments. Shown in the 3-color desert (DCU) cover worn with desert uniforms. During the 2000s the Army replaced it with the Advanced Combat Helmet.

credit.creator: U.S. Army Natick Research, Development and Engineering Center, 1991

name: ACH / MICH, bare tan
caption: Tan shell, no cover
note: Advanced Combat Helmet (ACH), developed from the Special Operations MICH. PEO Soldier says it has been in use since 2002 and replaced the PASGT. It is lighter than the PASGT and gives better fragment, ballistic and impact protection. It has pad suspension and a pre-drilled hole for a night-vision mount. Shells were painted in several colors, including tan, and were often worn without a cover.

credit.creator: MC1 James E. Foehl, U.S. Navy

name: ACH / MICH, ACU cover
caption: UCP cover and night-vision mount
note: The Advanced Combat Helmet in the Universal Camouflage Pattern (UCP) cover of the Army Combat Uniform, with a night-vision mount bracket on the front. This was the standard Army helmet look of the ACU years, from the mid-2000s.

name: JERRV (Cougar 6x6)
caption: Joint EOD Rapid Response Vehicle, desert tan
note: Joint EOD Rapid Response Vehicle (JERRV): the 6x6 Force Protection Cougar built as a mine-protected truck for explosive ordnance disposal teams, with a V-shaped hull that deflects blast away from the crew. The Navy's caption for this photo calls them “Cougar type JERRVs … employed by Coalition forces for escort and logistics missions, and to protect personnel from Improvised Explosive Devices.” Card photo: JERRVs of NMCB-7 in Iraq, 2008, with mine rollers.

name: John Deere M-Gator
caption: 6x4 military utility vehicle
note: John Deere M-Gator: a small 6x4 utility vehicle that carries two people and cargo, small enough to fly inside transport aircraft and helicopters. Card photo: Marines test-drive an M-Gator at Camp Leatherneck, Afghanistan, 2014.

credit.creator: Cpl. John Martinez, U.S. Marine Corps (2014)

name: Polaris Sportsman ATV
caption: Military all-terrain vehicle
note: Polaris Sportsman military all-terrain vehicle, a four-wheel quad used for light transport around bases and on patrol in Afghanistan. Card photo: a Polaris ATV at FOB Walton, Afghanistan, 2010.

name: Polaris Ranger UTV
caption: Side-by-side utility vehicle
note: Polaris Ranger: a side-by-side utility task vehicle (UTV) with a cargo bed, used for moving people and gear around bases. Card photo: a Ranger XP 1000 at Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base, 2023 (a newer model than the one he used).

name: Bobcat skid-steer loader
caption: Compact loader (bucket or forks)
note: Bobcat skid-steer loader: a compact loader that steers by turning its wheels at different speeds and takes a bucket, forks or other attachments. Card photo: a Bobcat on a Pacific Partnership engineering project, East Timor, 2008.

name: RHIB (rigid-hull inflatable boat)
caption: EODMU-5 dive RHIB, about this size
note: Rigid-hull inflatable boat: a solid hull with inflatable tubes around it, used by Navy EOD mobile units as a dive and work boat. Sergio used an EODMU-5 center-console dive RHIB of about this size; the exact length and maker are not confirmed. Card photo: EODMU-5 Detachment Japan tending divers from a RHIB, 2005.

credit.creator: Photographer's Mate 2nd Class John L. Beeman, U.S. Navy (2005)

name: AN/PRC-117F
caption: Harris multiband manpack radio
note: Harris AN/PRC-117F: a multiband manpack radio covering VHF and UHF, including UHF tactical satellite (TACSAT), with built-in COMSEC. Widely used by U.S. forces in the 2000s.

name: AN/PSC-5 (Spitfire)
caption: UHF tactical satellite radio; he used the -5D
note: AN/PSC-5 “Spitfire”: a lightweight UHF tactical satellite (TACSAT) and line-of-sight manpack radio. He used the AN/PSC-5D version; the card photo shows an airman assembling a PSC-5 at RAF Fairford, 2004.

credit.creator: Senior Airman Stacia M. Willis, U.S. Air Force (2004)

name: AN/PRC-148 MBITR
caption: Thales handheld radio
note: Thales AN/PRC-148 Multiband Inter/Intra Team Radio (MBITR): a handheld radio covering 30–512 MHz with embedded encryption, widely used by U.S. special operations forces.

name: Iridium 9505 satellite phone
caption: Handheld satellite phone
note: Motorola 9505 handset for the Iridium satellite network, which reaches almost anywhere on Earth through a constellation of low-orbit satellites.

credit.creator: Romeo (Wikimedia Commons user), released into the public domain

name: STE secure telephone
caption: Secure Terminal Equipment
note: Secure Terminal Equipment (STE): the U.S. government secure desk telephone that replaced the STU-III, encrypting calls with a Fortezza crypto card. Card photo: National Cryptologic Museum.

name: SWE-DISH flyaway terminal
caption: Portable satellite terminal
note: SWE-DISH flyaway satellite terminal: a small satellite dish that packs into transit cases and sets up in the field to give a team a satellite data link. Card photo: SWE-DISH FA150T military flyaway systems.

name: KOI-18
caption: General purpose tape reader (fill device)
note: KOI-18: a hand-held reader that pulls punched paper key tape through by hand and loads the key into crypto equipment. Card photo: National Cryptologic Museum.

name: KYK-13
caption: Electronic transfer device (fill device)
note: KYK-13: an electronic transfer device that holds up to six cryptographic keys and loads them into crypto equipment. Card photo: National Cryptologic Museum.

name: AN/CYZ-10 DTD
caption: Data transfer device (fill device)
note: AN/CYZ-10 Data Transfer Device, the “crazy 10”: a hand-held key-management device that stores and loads electronic keys, replacing the KYK-13 and KOI-18. Card photo: National Cryptologic Museum.

name: KL-43
caption: TRW keyboard crypto terminal; he used the KL-43C
note: KL-43: a small TRW battery-powered keyboard terminal that encrypts text messages off-line and sends them over a phone line or radio. He used the KL-43C version; the card photo shows a KL-43 at the National Cryptologic Museum.

name: TACLANE KG-175 / KG-175A
caption: General Dynamics in-line network encryptor
note: TACLANE (KG-175): the General Dynamics in-line network encryptor (INE) that secures IP traffic across untrusted networks. Card photo: a KG-175A and KG-175 at the National Cryptologic Museum.

name: KG-84 / KG-84A
caption: Dedicated loop encryption device
note: KG-84: a general-purpose encryption device for data links and dedicated loops. He used the KG-84A; the card photo shows a KG-84 at the National Cryptologic Museum.

name: KY-99A
caption: Secure voice equipment (KY-99 shown)
note: KY-99A: a green, ruggedized narrowband and wideband voice and data encryptor used with tactical radios, with audio, fill/data and radio ports on the front. It belongs to the same family as the KY-100. Card photo: the earlier KY-99 at the National Cryptologic Museum.

name: AN/PYQ-10 SKL
caption: Simple Key Loader
note: AN/PYQ-10 Simple Key Loader (SKL): a hand-held key loader that replaced the AN/CYZ-10 and stores, manages and loads electronic keys. Card photo: an SKL connected to an MV-22 avionics bay, Camp Bastion, 2011 (cropped).

credit.creator: Lance Cpl. Robert R. Carrasco, U.S. Marine Corps (2011)

name: JBLOX
caption: JCSE transit-case comms kit
note: JBLOX: a JCSE transit-case communications kit that, per the Joint Enabling Capabilities Command, “utilizes the latest virtual technology to provide communications capabilities ranging from early entry to the establishment of a joint task force.” Card photo: a JBLOX ashore during a USSOUTHCOM mission, 2013.

credit.creator: Richard Maupin, Joint Enabling Capabilities Command (2013)

name: JCSE IEP kit (Initial Entry Package)
caption: Small deployable comms package
note: JCSE's Initial Entry Package is, in DoD's words, “a small, joint communications package designed to provide secure and unsecured network access, voice and video capabilities.” Sergio recalls his tent kit (radio, IP phone, Toughbook and a PacStar-style case) as likely part of an IEP. Card photo: a JCSE IEP set up for paratroopers during Talisman Saber 13, Australia, 2013.

name: AN/PRC-150
caption: Harris HF manpack radio
note: Harris AN/PRC-150(C) Falcon II: a high-frequency (HF) manpack radio for long-range voice and data beyond line of sight, with embedded encryption. Used by U.S. forces in the 2000s; one of the two rack radios in his comms setup, with the PRC-117F.

name: Interceptor / IOTV, ACU (UCP)
caption: IOTV in UCP shown, with deltoid protectors
note: The Army's Interceptor Body Armor family in the Universal Camouflage Pattern (UCP) worn with the ACU. The Improved Outer Tactical Vest (IOTV), fielded from 2007, replaced the Interceptor Outer Tactical Vest. It carries front, back and side ballistic plates over soft armor. He wore this with the ACU on the C-RAM individual augmentee (IA) deployment. Card photo: an Army IOTV in UCP, 2008.

name: Plate carrier, MultiCam
caption: Soldier Plate Carrier System (SPCS) shown
note: A lighter plate carrier in MultiCam, worn in Afghanistan. It holds front and back ballistic plates with less soft armor coverage than the IOTV. The Army fielded the Soldier Plate Carrier System (SPCS) to units in Afghanistan from 2010. Card photo: a PEO Soldier SPCS in MultiCam, 2008 (his carrier's exact model is not recorded).
